title: QProfile snapshot: INT8 vs FP8 latency/quality review
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Medlytic through an Optimize console snapshot comparing INT8 vs FP8 qprofiles across latency and quality for their triage/summary workload. Covered benchmark methodology, representative prompt set, KV/prefix caching impact, and rollout strategy. Customer requested targeted benchmarks on 2k and 8k context lengths, security docs (SOC2/KMS), and a pilot pricing estimate. Next steps include Redwood sending benchmark spreadsheet, security pack, and scheduling a 1-week pilot run on Dedicated.
topics: latency regression modes and tail latency
benchmark methodology (prompt sets, seeds, eval metrics)
rollout strategy: canary + fallback to fp8

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we can get started. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, with Ben from our infra team. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Priya Singh: Hi Maya, thanks, excited to dig in. We got Sandra and Ethan here as well.
[00:00:12] Sandra Ruiz: Hey all. 
[00:00:14] Ben Ortega: Morning/afternoon, folks. We'll keep this focused on the Optimize qprofile snapshot and the INT8 vs FP8 tradeoffs.
[00:00:20] Ethan Cole: Quick note, we're joining from our SRE side, we'll listen for any infra constraints re VPC and private deployment.
[00:00:26] Maya Chen: Great. Outline: quick recap of the prompt set you shared, then walk through the console snapshot we ran, bench results, and then rollout options. Ben, want to take the console?
[00:00:35] Ben Ortega: Sure. So I pulled up the Optimize dashboard snapshot — apologies if some labels look different, our infra was updating names, so you might see "Optima" in one place— but this is the qprofile comparison for your triage/summarization workload. We ran INT8 and FP8 profiles on the 13B LLM variant you described, with the prompt set of 320 examples, mixture of short triage prompts (~150 tokens) and longer context ones up to 4k.
[00:01:00] Priya Singh: We also added 20 clinical examples, anonymized, to stress hallucination/faithfulness.
[00:01:06] Ben Ortega: Yup that was included. Important callouts up front: INT8 gave us ~35-42% token cost reduction and median latency improvements around 25% on hosted. FP8 sat between INT8 and FP16 in quality. But tail latency for INT8 showed more variance when KV cache misses and long context kicks in.
[00:01:30] Sandra Ruiz: When you say tail variance, what percentile are we looking at? 95th? 99th?
[00:01:35] Ben Ortega: We measured p50, p95, p99. INT8 p95 increased by ~180ms compared to FP8 on the 4k tests when prefix caching wasn't used. With prefix/KV caching enabled the gap shrank to ~60ms. So cache behavior matters a lot.
[00:01:51] Maya Chen: I'm going to share the benchmark spreadsheet link in the chat — it's the one we ran in the sandbox region with your config.
[00:01:57] Priya Singh: Got it. Seeing it now. The quality metrics — what's the eval metric? ROUGE or human L1?
[00:02:04] Ben Ortega: We used a mixed metric: automatic ROUGE-L and a small human-annotated fidelity score we ran on 60 clinical examples. The human score flagged hallucinations more frequently on INT8 in certain prompt formulations. But for short summarization INT8 was essentially parity.
[00:02:23] Ethan Cole: Are these runs on hosted or dedicated hardware? We prefer dedicated for sensitive PII workloads.
[00:02:29] Ben Ortega: These were hosted clusters but we've got a Dedicated run queued; results should be similar but you'll see slightly better latency consistency on Dedicated due to reserved GPU pools.
[00:02:39] Sandra Ruiz: Can you clarify the model variants? Are these compiled kernels or quantized weights? Any knob for per-layer precision?
[00:02:47] Ben Ortega: Good Q. These are post-training static quantization profiles — INT8 symmetric for most layers, with selective higher precision for attention output layers where we observed sensitivity. FP8 here is an automatic dynamic range FP8 profile using block-wise scaling. We also tried a hybrid qprofile where embedding and final MLP stayed at FP16. You can configure per-layer exceptions in the qprofile editor in Optimize.
[00:03:09] Priya Singh: That per-layer control is really helpful. For clinical prompts we might need to keep certain layers at FP16 to preserve factuality. How easy is it to roll that change out?
[00:03:18] Maya Chen: You can create a new qprofile, run a canary with 5% traffic or a pilot batch in the console, and we have automatic fallback to FP16/FP8 variants if accuracy regresses above a threshold. Ben, show the rollout controls?
[00:03:29] Ben Ortega: Yep. In this snapshot we used a canary of 10k tokens per minute for 24 hours with automatic rollback on quality deltas > 2.5 points on our audit metric. The console shows a quick diff view with sample outputs and an A/B eval.
[00:03:45] Ethan Cole: That rollback automation — does it tie into our incident channels / webhook? We need to pause rollout if SLOs degrade.
[00:03:51] Ben Ortega: It hooks into webhooks and you can bind it to PagerDuty or your internal webhook to create incidents. The rollout rules are scriptable via API too.
[00:03:59] Priya Singh: About quality deltas — can we run our own reference eval set? Ideally keep our clinical bench proprietary.
[00:04:06] Ben Ortega: Absolutely. You can upload a private eval set in the console (it stays in your VPC for private deployments) and we run the same eval harness against it. For hosted we treat uploads as customer-provided data with encryption at rest via KMS.
[00:04:20] Sandra Ruiz: Security questions: SOC 2, KMS, audit logs— do you have SOC 2 Type II? And for Dedicated/Private do the logs still go to Redwood?
[00:04:28] Maya Chen: We are SOC 2 Type II compliant. For Dedicated and Private deployments, logs can be forwarded to your logging stack or stored in your S3 buckets; we can configure audit log retention and integrate with your KMS/HSM. We'll share the security pack after this call.
[00:04:40] Priya Singh: Thanks. Next, the 8k context lane — you mentioned 4k earlier, can you explain differences when we move to 8k?
[00:04:47] Ben Ortega: Sure. Sequence length increases memory pressure and affects kernel selection. INT8 gives better throughput per GPU but KV cache hits/misses become more expensive at 8k. FP8 held up better on hallucination-sensitive prompts but cost more. We saw median latency on 8k go up for INT8 by ~30% vs FP8 when we weren't using prefix chunking. When we applied prefix chunking and streaming with incremental KV writes the gap reduced.
[00:05:09] Ethan Cole: So engineering-wise we should instrument caching and prefer warm-started sessions?
[00:05:14] Ben Ortega: Exactly, warm KV cache and using predictable prompt patterns helps INT8 shine. For ad-hoc long contexts FP8 is safer initially.
[00:05:22] Priya Singh: On hallucination examples, can you show a sample diff between INT8 and FP8 output?
[00:05:25] Ben Ortega: Yep — pulling up sample diffs. (brief pause) You can see for prompt #17 INT8 added a confident but incorrect medication dosing; FP8 kept to the text and recommended checking the chart. We highlight these in the diff view and tag them for your reviewers.
[00:05:44] Maya Chen: Note that these are edge cases and we usually tune qprofiles to avoid that layer or adjust temperature/formatting. Also caching sometimes changes the prompt composition which affects hallucination rates.
[00:05:55] Priya Singh: Good to know. On the cost side, you said tokens cost reduction 35-42% — is that purely model compute or does it factor in infra egress/storage?
[00:06:03] Ben Ortega: That's model compute only. We also modeled end-to-end unit economics in the spreadsheet including bandwidth and memory overheads; the hosted SKU shows the largest gains given multi-tenant batching. Dedicated has smaller percentage gains but more predictable spend.
[00:06:18] Sandra Ruiz: If we do a pilot on Dedicated, how long to spin up capacity? We have procurement timelines.
[00:06:25] Maya Chen: Dedicated provisioning for a pilot (small GPU pool) typically takes 5-7 business days once contract is signed. We can start a hosted pilot faster if time-to-data is critical.
[00:06:34] Ethan Cole: Procurement will want an estimate. Can you send a pilot pricing sheet?
[00:06:37] Maya Chen: Absolutely, we'll include pilot pricing in the follow-up email.
[00:06:41] Ben Ortega: One more technical note — quantization sensitivity sweep: we ran layer-wise sensitivity and found the attention output and final MLP layers were the most sensitive on your model. For those we kept higher precision in the hybrid profile. We can attach the sensitivity heatmap.
[00:06:56] Priya Singh: Please do. Also, is there an automated quality monitor to detect regressions in production?
[00:07:03] Ben Ortega: Yes — Redwood Optimize supports continuous quality monitoring: you can attach prompt sinks and label a small sample via human review; the system alerts when regression thresholds are crossed and can trigger rollbacks.
[00:07:13] Sandra Ruiz: Do we need to send data to Redwood for that? We're strict about PHI.
[00:07:17] Ben Ortega: For PHI we recommend Dedicated or Private. In Private deployments, the monitoring agent runs in your VPC and only metadata and aggregated metrics leave your environment if you opt in.
[00:07:27] Maya Chen: Okay let's talk deliverables — Ben, can you summarize what we agreed to run as follow-up benches?
[00:07:33] Ben Ortega: Sure: 1) 2k and 8k context deterministic bench comparing INT8, FP8, hybrid with your proprietary clinical eval set (private). 2) Dedicated spin-up smoke test to compare p95/p99 on reserved GPUs. 3) Latency tail analysis with and without prefix/KV caching. We'll provide the bench scripts and the spreadsheet.
[00:07:53] Priya Singh: Timeline?
[00:07:55] Ben Ortega: We can deliver initial bench results in 5 business days for hosted; Dedicated results after provision (~7-10 business days).
[00:08:03] Priya Singh: Great. Also can you include a config JSON for the qprofile we recommended? We want to version it in our repo.
[00:08:09] Ben Ortega: Yep we export qprofiles as JSON and will attach it.
[00:08:13] Ethan Cole: Any concerns about model drift or retraining? We tune qprofiles but model updates could change sensitivities.
[00:08:18] Maya Chen: We recommend re-running the sensitivity sweep as part of any model change; Optimize has a job template for that. We'll add that to the runbook we share.
[00:08:26] Sandra Ruiz: Who's the contact for security review?
[00:08:28] Maya Chen: I'll be primary AE; for technical security Ben and our security eng Emily Park will be on the thread. We'll send SOC2 report, KMS integration guide, and private deployment checklist.
[00:08:39] Priya Singh: Perfect. I have one last small ask — can you run a low-latency tail test with bufferized batching settings? We think batching may hurt our interactive UX.
[00:08:48] Ben Ortega: Yes, we'll run both batching off and with micro-batching and share p50/p95/p99.
[00:08:55] Maya Chen: Okay we're at about 9 minutes, want to open for quick Qs before recap?
[00:09:00] Priya Singh: Quick ops Q — will the qprofile changes require a model reload? Or RCD?
[00:09:05] Ben Ortega: Minor changes can be hot-swapped; larger structural quant changes trigger a model variant build which can be rolled out without downtime via canary.
[00:09:13] Ethan Cole: Good.
[00:09:15] Sandra Ruiz: Thanks, that's clear.
[00:09:18] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to send bench spreadsheet, qprofile JSON, security pack (SOC2/KMS/HSM/audit logs), pilot pricing, and schedule Dedicated spin-up demo once contract signed. Customer to confirm internal eval dataset upload and pilot approval timeline.
[00:09:33] Priya Singh: We'll aim to confirm dataset upload this week.
[00:09:37] Ethan Cole: Procurement will need the pilot price by Friday.
[00:09:40] Maya Chen: Noted. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the Dedicated demo.
[00:09:47] Sandra Ruiz: Thanks all.
[00:09:50] Meeting end (automated)
